I look around at my family gathered at home, thinking through what I know. The upkeep bill is due—450 sim for the household, plus my own 150 head tax. That's 600 sim, and I hold 500. I already know I'm short, and I know Perrin told me about 400 sim set aside. It's costing me to keep that knowledge to myself, but I'm more curious about something else right now.

I need to understand what's happening with the debt and the marker. Both houses are tiptoeing around it, and nobody will say what they know. I can see the shape of it—Perrin wouldn't have mentioned that money if it weren't connected to something larger.

"Why don't you just tell me what the marker is for?" I ask aloud, not directing it at anyone in particular, just wanting to see who flinches. "Can I ask something? The debt's not just going to wait because we all pretend not to have noticed it."

But I'm also practical. I'm heading to college soon, and I need to sort my own finances first. The household debt will get paid or it won't—that's not just my problem to solve. But my head tax is.

I turn to my parents and siblings. "I'm borrowing 100 sim," I say simply, holding out my hand. "I'll pay it back when I earn. I need to clear my tax today." It's a statement, not a request with room for refusal. I know my family well enough—they might grumble, but they'll give. They always do when I don't make them work for it by asking twice.

Then I'll eat something—whatever's on hand—and head toward college. Perrin will be waiting, and we have things to say to each other that our houses won't.

Let me call the tools to make this happen: I said it out loud. Let me see who flinches, then deal with my immediate need:  I've spoken. Now I wait to see if anyone responds with the money I need—or with something about the debt I just named.
